nodes.title: What personality trait means
nodes.body:
A tendency that appears with some consistency across situations. One behaviour is a clue, not a complete measure of a trait.

For example: Someone regularly seeks recognition in different groups over many months.

One important limit: A single boast after good news is not a stable personality description.

nodes.title: What defensiveness means
nodes.body:
An attempt to protect oneself from information that feels threatening. It can appear in anyone, especially when something important feels at risk.

For example: A worker argues sharply when asked to correct the credit on a presentation.

One important limit: Defensiveness does not reveal whether the criticism was fair or whether the person has a disorder.

nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.

nodes.scenario: Maya built the statistical analysis. Leo led the project. The final slide credits only Leo.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Could we change the slide? It says you developed the analysis, but that was my work.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I thought we'd agreed I was taking ownership of the results.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Of presenting them, yes. I still think the analysis should be credited accurately.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: You don't understand what's riding on this. They're considering me for a promotion.

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
checks.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Why does criticism feel like an attack?
lessons.teach: A presentation is about to go to senior management. Maya completed the analysis; Leo leads the team and is credited with work she did. When Maya asks for an accurate correction, Leo responds as if his professional standing is at risk. In this lesson you will examine the same exchange the way a careful psychologist would: start with observable evidence, build competing explanations, look for what maintains the response, and update your judgement when new messages come to light. You'll finish by applying the reasoning to an unfamiliar relationship.
lessons.objective: Identify observable evidence of self-worth threat, explain a plausible defensive cycle, distinguish function from conscious intention, revise hypotheses when new evidence appears, and select a proportionate response in a fresh situation.

nodes.title: One correction, several possible meanings
nodes.body:
Maya completed the statistical analysis for a team project. Leo managed the team and is presenting the results to senior management. A slide claims Leo developed the analysis. Maya asks for the credit to be corrected before the presentation is sent.

This is a useful case because we can examine an ordinary-looking disagreement without assuming that the explanation is obvious. Leo may feel criticised. He may also stand to gain professionally from leaving the slide unchanged. Those possibilities can both be relevant.

By the end, you should be able to identify what is actually observed, explain how a threat to self-worth might produce defensiveness, revise an interpretation when new evidence arrives, and choose a response that protects Maya's interests. None of those tasks requires diagnosing Leo.

nodes.title: Why can a correction feel bigger than the correction?
nodes.body:
Think of self-worth as the value someone believes they have as a person. Some people can hear, “This slide is inaccurate,” without treating it as an assessment of their competence. For others, being seen as especially capable may carry a great deal of personal meaning.

Psychologists sometimes call this **contingent self-worth**: feeling valuable depends heavily on meeting a condition, such as receiving approval or appearing successful. When the condition feels threatened, defending it can become more urgent than considering the original issue.

Leo does not say “I am worthless unless I look capable.” We cannot assume that thought is present. What he does say is that a correction might make senior colleagues doubt his ability. That makes threatened professional identity a reasonable working explanation.

A working explanation is a proposal that fits the available facts and can change when new information arrives. We have not discovered a hidden fact about Leo's personality. We have identified a process worth investigating.

nodes.title: Where narcissism enters the picture
nodes.body:
Clinical researchers have long studied forms of narcissism in which a person's self-esteem is difficult to maintain without outside recognition. Two broad experiences often discussed are **grandiosity**, involving a strong need to appear exceptional, and **vulnerability**, involving sensitivity to feeling inadequate or exposed. They can overlap in the same person. Neither can be confidently identified from a single office argument.

A 2010 review by Pincus and Lukowitsky describes disagreements between clinical definitions and research measures of pathological narcissism. The Pathological Narcissism Inventory, developed by Pincus and colleagues in 2009, was one attempt to measure grandiose and vulnerable expressions more fully. A 2024 systematic review examined how pathological narcissism relates to difficulties regulating emotion; findings depend on how these constructs are defined and measured.

What does this contribute to Leo's case? It gives us a plausible account of why criticism might provoke self-protection when recognition is central to someone's self-worth. It does **not** establish that Leo has pathological narcissism. The distinction between a momentary defensive response, a recurring personality tendency, and a clinical disorder requires much more information.

It also cannot erase Maya's position. She produced the analysis. The slide is inaccurate. Leo's internal experience may help us understand his response, while his responsibility for correcting the attribution remains.

nodes.title: What an explanation must leave room for
nodes.body:
An explanation becomes useful when it distinguishes between competing possibilities. If Leo had consistently described the work as a joint responsibility and had never acknowledged Maya's role, confusion about attribution would remain comparatively strong. The earlier message changes that balance.

We should also separate **function** from **intention**. The function of a response is what it achieves. Leo's refusal may help him avoid embarrassment even if he does not deliberately set out to regulate an uncomfortable feeling. Intention asks what he was consciously trying to accomplish. A behaviour can have more than one function, and a conscious career incentive can exist alongside an emotional one.

This is how clinical formulation differs from casual labelling. A formulation links a specific situation with an interpretation, a response and its consequences. It remains revisable when better evidence arrives. A diagnostic assessment asks a broader question about lasting patterns and impairment. Neither should be replaced by guessing someone's whole personality from one conflict.

nodes.title: What you can now take into real life
nodes.body:
When a person reacts strongly to a correction, begin with what they actually said and did. Ask what the disagreement seems to put at stake. Then consider what their response achieves in the moment and what it might cost later.

In this case, Leo fears that recognising Maya's work could threaten his image as a capable leader. That offers a plausible account of his defensiveness. The later messages give stronger evidence that he knowingly claimed the analysis. Both observations belong in the explanation.

The practical lesson is equally important. Maya does not have to establish why Leo is doing this before protecting her contribution. Clear evidence and a proportionate request can help her decide what to do next.

A good psychological account should sharpen your judgement. It should tell you what you know, what remains uncertain, and what would provide a fairer next step.

glossary.definition: A tendency that appears with some consistency across situations. One behaviour is a clue, not a complete measure of a trait.
glossary.example: Someone regularly seeks recognition in different groups over many months.
glossary.limit: A single boast after good news is not a stable personality description.

glossary.definition: An attempt to protect oneself from information that feels threatening. It can appear in anyone, especially when something important feels at risk.
glossary.example: A worker argues sharply when asked to correct the credit on a presentation.
glossary.limit: Defensiveness does not reveal whether the criticism was fair or whether the person has a disorder.

glossary.definition: When feeling acceptable or valuable depends heavily on meeting a particular condition, such as appearing competent.
glossary.example: A small correction feels like proof of being a failure because reputation carries enormous weight.
glossary.limit: Wanting approval is common; the extent and cost of dependence matter.

glossary.definition: A clinical pattern considered through its persistence, pervasiveness and effects on functioning. It requires much more evidence than one argument.
glossary.example: A clinician investigates a long history across relationships before making any diagnostic judgement.
glossary.limit: A difficult interaction cannot establish a diagnosis, and a diagnosis cannot explain every action.
